title: Maria Renata Singer von Mossau Executed in Würzburg: Last Major German Execution
description:
Maria Renata Singer von Mossau, a sub-prioress of the Premonstratensian convent of Unterzell near Würzburg, was executed on June 21, 1749 — beheaded and then burned — following her conviction for witchcraft and the alleged bewitchment of several nuns in her convent. The case was unusual in the mid-eighteenth century both for its scale of seriousness and for the specific context of conventual possession: Maria Renata was accused not only of practicing witchcraft herself but of having introduced the demonic infection into the convent, causing the possession symptoms displayed by other nuns. The prosecution was initiated by secular authorities, with the local prince-bishop's court taking the lead, over the objections of more cautious Church officials who were aware of the controversy such a prosecution would generate.

The case attracted immediate European controversy precisely because witch prosecution was by 1749 widely seen as anachronistic. The Bavarian court issued a post-trial edict expressing disapproval of the proceeding, and various Enlightenment commentators used the case as evidence of the persistence of superstition in Catholic territories. The Jesuit who preached at Maria Renata's execution published a sermon defending the proceeding that became a target of mockery and attack in Enlightenment circles, including by Voltaire. Maria Renata's execution thus became one of the defining Enlightenment anecdotes about clerical superstition and judicial barbarism.

Historians have been cautious about treating this as definitively the 'last' German witch execution, noting that lesser-documented cases may have occurred. However, its scale (an execution, not merely a prosecution), its documentation, and the controversy it generated make it a significant marker of the late survival of witchcraft prosecution in Germany. Lyndal Roper's work on German witchcraft situates the 1749 case within the long aftermath of the German prosecutions.
historiographical_note: The Maria Renata case has been analyzed as a test case for Enlightenment attitudes toward witch prosecution. Wolfgang Behringer's work on German witch-hunting provides context for the survival of prosecution impulses in Catholic areas of Germany into the mid-eighteenth century. Lyndal Roper's Witch Craze (2004) discusses the long legacy of German witch-hunting. The Enlightenment use of the case — particularly Voltaire's commentary — is analyzed in studies of eighteenth-century anti-clerical polemic.
source_method: Contemporary printed accounts including Gaar's execution sermon; published scholarship on German witchcraft
